plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three U-tube manometer configurations that together cover every possible relationship between gas pressure and atmospheric pressure, each labeled with the corresponding pressure equation below. The left panel depicts a closed-end manometer whose sealed arm contains a vacuum, making the height difference h the sole determinant of pressure so that P_gas = hρg. The middle panel shows an open-end manometer in which the gas-side liquid stands higher than the open (atmospheric) side, indicating the gas is below atmospheric pressure and P_gas = P_atm − hρg. The right panel reverses that situation — the open-arm liquid is higher — indicating the gas exceeds atmospheric pressure so that P_gas = P_atm + hρg. This figure introduces the manometer as a practical pressure-measuring instrument and establishes the three distinct cases that determine which formula relates the liquid-column height h to the unknown gas pressure.

interactionPlan.concept: A manometer measures an unknown gas pressure by balancing it against a mercury column, and which of three equations applies (P_gas = hρg, P_atm − hρg, or P_atm + hρg) depends entirely on whether the reference arm is a vacuum or open to the atmosphere and which arm's mercury stands higher.
elements: Three side-by-side manometer panels (left: closed-end; middle: open-end with gas below atmospheric; right: open-end with gas above atmospheric)
Spherical gas bulb labeled 'Gas' (pale lavender fill, gray outline) at upper left of each panel
Stopcock / valve glyph on the horizontal tube between the bulb and the U-tube
Horizontal connecting tube descending into the left arm of the U-tube
U-shaped glass tube with two vertical arms joined by a rounded bottom bend, drawn as a light-blue-gray outlined channel
Mercury fill shown as dark gray liquid occupying the bend and part of both arms; empty tube above the mercury shown pale lavender (gas side) or pale blue-gray (reference side)
Left panel: sealed top of right arm with leader labels 'Closed end' and 'Vacuum'
Middle and right panels: open top of right arm with a downward arrow labeled 'P_atm' and a leader label 'Open end'
Horizontal tick lines marking the mercury meniscus level in each arm
Double-headed vertical arrow spanning the two meniscus levels, labeled with italic 'h' (long span in left and middle panels, short span near the top in the right panel)
Equation caption under each panel: 'P_gas = hρg', 'P_gas = P_atm − hρg', 'P_gas = P_atm + hρg'
Numeric readout overlay: current P_gas, P_atm (760 torr), and h in mm Hg
Derivation callout box (hidden until the h arrow is clicked) listing the force-balance steps for the active configuration
Highlight ring / colored box around whichever equation is currently active

interactions.label: Manometer configuration
interactions.teaches: That the same instrument yields three different equations depending on whether the reference arm is evacuated or open, and on which mercury column stands higher.

interactions.label: Gas pressure P_gas (torr)
interactions.teaches: That h is not a fixed drawing but a direct readout of the pressure difference: raising P_gas pushes mercury away from the gas arm, and in open-end mode the columns cross over exactly when P_gas = P_atm, flipping which formula applies.
interactions.default_note: In open-end mode, crossing 760 torr automatically switches the active panel and the highlighted equation.

interactions.teaches: Clicking the h arrow reveals the force balance at the lowest mercury level — pressure pushing down on one side equals pressure pushing down on the other — from which each of the three equations is derived rather than memorized.

demo_steps.title: Three cases, one instrument
demo_steps.narration: All three drawings are the same U-tube of mercury connected to a gas bulb; only the far arm and the liquid levels differ. Each configuration carries its own equation for P_gas.

demo_steps.title: Closed end: mercury measures pressure outright
demo_steps.narration: With the far arm sealed and evacuated, nothing pushes back on the mercury from above, so the entire height difference h is produced by the gas alone: P_gas = hρg.

demo_steps.title: Raise the gas pressure
demo_steps.narration: Drag P_gas upward and watch h grow in exact proportion. In a closed-end manometer, h in millimeters of mercury IS the gas pressure in torr.

demo_steps.title: Open end, gas below atmospheric
demo_steps.narration: Now the far arm feels P_atm pushing down. Because the gas is weaker, atmospheric pressure drives mercury toward the gas side, leaving that column higher: P_gas = P_atm − hρg.

demo_steps.title: Open end, gas above atmospheric
demo_steps.narration: Push P_gas past 760 torr and the columns swap: the gas shoves mercury up the open arm, so the extra height adds to atmospheric pressure, giving P_gas = P_atm + hρg.

demo_steps.title: Where the equations come from
demo_steps.narration: Click the h arrow to see the force balance at the lowest mercury level — every one of the three formulas is just 'pressure down on the left = pressure down on the right' rearranged.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A manometer never measures pressure directly — it measures a pressure DIFFERENCE as a mercury height; whether you add h, subtract h, or use h alone depends only on what is pressing down on the other arm (vacuum or atmosphere) and which column ended up higher.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Three panels arranged left to right on a white background, each roughly the same size and vertically aligned. Each panel: a pale lavender circle labeled 'Gas' at upper left with a gray outline, a small screw-style stopcock glyph on the short horizontal tube leading right, then the tube turns down into the left arm of a tall U-tube with a rounded bottom. Tube walls drawn as thin light blue-gray double lines; mercury rendered as a solid medium-dark gray column filling the bend and rising partway up each arm; the space above mercury on the gas side tinted pale lavender, on the reference side pale blue-gray. Left panel's right arm is sealed at the top with two leader lines labeled 'Closed end' and 'Vacuum'; middle and right panels show an open tube top with a short black downward arrow labeled 'P_atm' and a leader labeled 'Open end'. Thin horizontal rules mark each meniscus level, connected by a slim double-headed vertical arrow annotated with italic 'h' — a long span in the left and middle panels (gas-arm mercury higher in the middle panel) and a short span high on the tube in the right panel (open-arm mercury higher). Italic serif equations centered beneath each panel: P_gas = hρg, P_gas = P_atm − hρg, P_gas = P_atm + hρg. Active configuration highlighted with a soft colored box around its panel and equation; inactive panels dimmed. Mercury levels must animate continuously with the pressure slider, conserving total mercury volume between arms, and the h label plus a torr readout must update live.

authoredContext:
A manometer is a device similar to a barometer that can be used to measure the pressure of a gas trapped in a container. A closed-end manometer is a U-shaped tube with one closed arm, one arm that connects to the gas to be measured, and a nonvolatile liquid (usually mercury) in between. As with a barometer, the distance between the liquid levels in the two arms of the tube ( h in the diagram) is proportional to the pressure of the gas in the container. An open-end manometer ( ) is the same as a closed-end manometer, but one of its arms is open to the atmosphere. In this case, the distance between the liquid levels corresponds to the difference in pressure between the gas in the container and the atmosphere.

A manometer can be used to measure the pressure of a gas. The (difference in) height between the liquid levels ( h ) is a measure of the pressure. Mercury is usually used because of its large density.

Three diagrams of manometers are shown. Each manometer consists of a spherical pink container filled with gas on the left that is connected to a U-shaped, sealed tube by a valve on its right. The top of the U aligns with the gas-filled sphere and the U, which extends below, contains mercury. The first manometer has a sealed tube. The sealed end to the upper right in the diagram is labeled “closed end” and “vacuum.” The mercury level is higher in the right side of the tube than in the left. The difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign h rho g. The second manometer has an open-ended tube, which is labeled “open end.” At this opening in the upper right of the diagram is the label P subscript atm. The mercury level is higher in the left side of the tube than in the right. This difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign P subscript atm minus sign h rho g. The third manometer has an open-ended tube and is similar to the second manometer except that the mercury level is higher in the right side of the tube than in the left. This difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign P subscript a t m plus h rho g.

discrepancies: All text is rendered very small relative to the drawing (16px inside a 1240-wide viewBox scaled to ~600px), so 'Closed end', 'Vacuum', 'Open end', the P_gas equations and the h labels are barely readable at inline size, whereas in the source these labels are prominent.

Extra annotations not in the source: a grey 'P_atm = 760 torr' note in the top-left corner and a numeric readout line ('P_gas = 760 torr · h = 760 mm Hg') beneath each equation, which crowd the captions.
The h label in the third (high-pressure) panel is pushed to the right of the arrow with a tiny leader tick, unlike the source where h sits cleanly between the two level lines next to the arrow.

Glass/mercury rendering is flatter than the source: the source tubes show a pale lavender-blue glass wall with a shaded grey mercury column and clearly flared open-tube lips; the generated version uses uniform strokes and only small tick marks for the open-end lip.
Level rule lines extend the same distance on all panels; in the source the rule lines and arrow offsets differ slightly per panel (longer for the tall h in panels 1–2, very short in panel 3).
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful three-panel manometer set with correct level directions, correct equations and a rich, working set of interactions (config select, pressure slider with tweened mercury, derivation toggle, 6-step demo, tooltips/popups); main weakness is label legibility — all annotation text is far too small relative to the drawing — plus some added numeric clutter not in the source.
action_items: Increase annotation font sizes (labels ~22–24, equations ~28 in the 1240-wide viewBox) or shrink the viewBox so 'Closed end', 'Vacuum', 'Open end', P_atm and the h labels read comfortably at inline width.
Remove or de-emphasise the per-panel numeric readout line and the corner 'P_atm = 760 torr' note (move them into the tooltip/UI panel) so the captions match the source's clean equation-only look.
Place the h label consistently between the two level rules beside the arrow in all three panels, using a short offset only when the gap is genuinely too small, and avoid the extra leader tick.
Refine the tube rendering: add the flared lip at the open ends, a subtle shading/gradient on the mercury column, and the pale lavender glass tint of the source for closer visual match.
Avoid clamping the h displacement (DMAX) within the normal slider range so the h ∝ P proportionality stays exact across the full 0–1520 torr sweep.

feedback.rationale: The concept, panel structure, and interaction set are correct; the remaining issues are implementation details like font sizing, label placement, extraneous readouts, and tube styling.

discrepancies: Text is rendered at a small effective size: a 1240-wide viewbox scaled into a ~595 px panel makes 'Closed end', 'Vacuum', 'Open end' and the caption equations roughly 10–13 px on screen, noticeably less legible than the prominent annotations in the source.

In the third panel (P_gas > P_atm) the small level gap makes the italic 'h' label sit almost on top of the double-headed arrow and the two level rules, whereas the source keeps 'h' cleanly to the left of the arrow with clear spacing.

Equation captions render with tight subscript kerning ('P gas= hρg' / 'Pgas= Patm− hρg') so the spacing around '=' and the subscript baseline differs visibly from the clean typeset equations in the source.
The drawing sits in the upper-left of a much taller white container, leaving a large empty band below the equations that is not present in the source's tight three-panel composition.
Level-indicator rules in the generated figure extend well to the right of the tube (to a fixed x), slightly longer/heavier than the short horizontal tick rules in the source.
evaluation.notes: A faithful three-panel manometer reproduction with correct tube topology, mercury shading, level relationships and all three equations, backed by genuinely useful slider/dropdown/step/derivation interactions; main weaknesses are undersized annotation text at inline scale, crowding of the 'h' label in the narrow third panel, and wasted vertical whitespace.

Offset the 'h' label outward (or place it beside an extended arrow) when the level gap is small so it no longer overlaps the arrow and level rules in the P_gas > P_atm panel.
Fix subscript kerning in runText (add a small advance after subscript runs) so captions read 'P_gas = P_atm − hρg' with spacing matching the source.
Shorten the meniscus level rules to match the short ticks in the source and reduce their stroke weight relative to the h arrow.

plan.concept: A manometer measures an unknown gas pressure by balancing it against a mercury column, and which of three equations applies (P_gas = hρg, P_atm − hρg, or P_atm + hρg) depends entirely on whether the reference arm is a vacuum or open to the atmosphere and which arm's mercury stands higher.
elements: Three side-by-side manometer panels (left: closed-end; middle: open-end with gas below atmospheric; right: open-end with gas above atmospheric)
Spherical gas bulb labeled 'Gas' (pale lavender fill, gray outline) at upper left of each panel
Stopcock / valve glyph on the horizontal tube between the bulb and the U-tube
Horizontal connecting tube descending into the left arm of the U-tube
U-shaped glass tube with two vertical arms joined by a rounded bottom bend, drawn as a light-blue-gray outlined channel
Mercury fill shown as dark gray liquid occupying the bend and part of both arms; empty tube above the mercury shown pale lavender (gas side) or pale blue-gray (reference side)
Left panel: sealed top of right arm with leader labels 'Closed end' and 'Vacuum'
Middle and right panels: open top of right arm with a downward arrow labeled 'P_atm' and a leader label 'Open end'
Horizontal tick lines marking the mercury meniscus level in each arm
Double-headed vertical arrow spanning the two meniscus levels, labeled with italic 'h' (long span in left and middle panels, short span near the top in the right panel)
Equation caption under each panel: 'P_gas = hρg', 'P_gas = P_atm − hρg', 'P_gas = P_atm + hρg'
Numeric readout overlay: current P_gas, P_atm (760 torr), and h in mm Hg
Derivation callout box (hidden until the h arrow is clicked) listing the force-balance steps for the active configuration
Highlight ring / colored box around whichever equation is currently active

interactions.label: Manometer configuration
interactions.teaches: That the same instrument yields three different equations depending on whether the reference arm is evacuated or open, and on which mercury column stands higher.

interactions.label: Gas pressure P_gas (torr)
interactions.teaches: That h is not a fixed drawing but a direct readout of the pressure difference: raising P_gas pushes mercury away from the gas arm, and in open-end mode the columns cross over exactly when P_gas = P_atm, flipping which formula applies.
interactions.default_note: In open-end mode, crossing 760 torr automatically switches the active panel and the highlighted equation.

interactions.teaches: Clicking the h arrow reveals the force balance at the lowest mercury level — pressure pushing down on one side equals pressure pushing down on the other — from which each of the three equations is derived rather than memorized.

demo_steps.title: Three cases, one instrument
demo_steps.narration: All three drawings are the same U-tube of mercury connected to a gas bulb; only the far arm and the liquid levels differ. Each configuration carries its own equation for P_gas.

demo_steps.title: Closed end: mercury measures pressure outright
demo_steps.narration: With the far arm sealed and evacuated, nothing pushes back on the mercury from above, so the entire height difference h is produced by the gas alone: P_gas = hρg.

demo_steps.title: Raise the gas pressure
demo_steps.narration: Drag P_gas upward and watch h grow in exact proportion. In a closed-end manometer, h in millimeters of mercury IS the gas pressure in torr.

demo_steps.title: Open end, gas below atmospheric
demo_steps.narration: Now the far arm feels P_atm pushing down. Because the gas is weaker, atmospheric pressure drives mercury toward the gas side, leaving that column higher: P_gas = P_atm − hρg.

demo_steps.title: Open end, gas above atmospheric
demo_steps.narration: Push P_gas past 760 torr and the columns swap: the gas shoves mercury up the open arm, so the extra height adds to atmospheric pressure, giving P_gas = P_atm + hρg.

demo_steps.title: Where the equations come from
demo_steps.narration: Click the h arrow to see the force balance at the lowest mercury level — every one of the three formulas is just 'pressure down on the left = pressure down on the right' rearranged.

plan.keyInsight: A manometer never measures pressure directly — it measures a pressure DIFFERENCE as a mercury height; whether you add h, subtract h, or use h alone depends only on what is pressing down on the other arm (vacuum or atmosphere) and which column ended up higher.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Three panels arranged left to right on a white background, each roughly the same size and vertically aligned. Each panel: a pale lavender circle labeled 'Gas' at upper left with a gray outline, a small screw-style stopcock glyph on the short horizontal tube leading right, then the tube turns down into the left arm of a tall U-tube with a rounded bottom. Tube walls drawn as thin light blue-gray double lines; mercury rendered as a solid medium-dark gray column filling the bend and rising partway up each arm; the space above mercury on the gas side tinted pale lavender, on the reference side pale blue-gray. Left panel's right arm is sealed at the top with two leader lines labeled 'Closed end' and 'Vacuum'; middle and right panels show an open tube top with a short black downward arrow labeled 'P_atm' and a leader labeled 'Open end'. Thin horizontal rules mark each meniscus level, connected by a slim double-headed vertical arrow annotated with italic 'h' — a long span in the left and middle panels (gas-arm mercury higher in the middle panel) and a short span high on the tube in the right panel (open-arm mercury higher). Italic serif equations centered beneath each panel: P_gas = hρg, P_gas = P_atm − hρg, P_gas = P_atm + hρg. Active configuration highlighted with a soft colored box around its panel and equation; inactive panels dimmed. Mercury levels must animate continuously with the pressure slider, conserving total mercury volume between arms, and the h label plus a torr readout must update live.

discrepancies: Equation captions render the subscript with an unusually wide gap ("P  gas = hρg" instead of a tight "P_gas"), so the typography reads noticeably looser than the source's compact italic labels.

In the third panel the h label is pushed outboard to the right of the arrow with a leader line, whereas the source places h immediately beside/left of the short double arrow inside the tube region; the two thin level rules there also sit very close to the 'Open end' leader line.

The 'Closed end' / 'Vacuum' leader polylines are shorter and bend differently from the source's long single-segment leaders, and the closed-arm sealed tip is drawn as a rounded stroke cap rather than the source's distinctly sealed rounded tube end.

The optional derivation callout boxes are placed at x 238–394 within a 388-px panel pitch, so they can overlap the neighbouring panel's gas bulb and the third box nearly reaches the viewbox edge (element not in the source, and a collision risk when toggled on).
Overall figure is rendered noticeably smaller/narrower than the source relative to the available canvas, leaving large empty margins above and below the three panels.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-composed reproduction of the three-panel mercury manometer figure with correct column-height physics and a rich, genuinely functional set of interactions (pressure slider, configuration selector, derivation toggle, 6-step demo); weaknesses are typographic spacing in the equation subscripts, a slightly displaced h label in panel 3, and derivation callouts that can spill into adjacent panels.

Keep the h label adjacent to the double arrow in the small-gap case (offset it upward/downward rather than 50 px to the right with a leader) and shorten the two level rules so they don't crowd the 'Open end' leader.
Reposition/size the derivation callout boxes so they stay inside each panel's 388-px pitch and never overlap the neighbouring bulb or the viewbox edge.
Scale the three panels up (or reduce vertical margin) so the drawing fills more of the canvas and label text reads comfortably at inline size.
